title: At the doctor
goal: Describe your symptoms at a Swedish health center, understand the doctor's instructions, and know whom to call when you're sick.
bekal: the body, from *huvud* to *fot*, with the irregular plurals
the modal verbs in action: *måste*, *bör*, *behöver inte*, *får inte*
wave: Go back to Unit 11: say five sentences about your week with *borde*, *behöver inte*, *slipper*, *brukar* and *får inte* — today's doctor uses the same verbs.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På vårdcentralen
dialogs.intro: Dian has had a sore throat and a fever since Sunday. On Wednesday she calls 1177, the healthcare advice line, and the nurse books her an appointment at the local health center on Södermalm the same afternoon.

notes: **Jag har ont i halsen** — literally "I have pain in the throat". This is the all-purpose way to say something hurts: *ont i huvudet* (headache), *ont i magen* (stomachache), *ont i ryggen* (backache). Notice that Swedish uses the **definite** form of the body part where English uses "my": *ont i hals**en***, not *ont i min hals*. **oont**.

**Jag mådde illa** — careful: *må illa* doesn't mean "to be ill" but "to feel sick to your stomach, to be nauseous". For "I feel unwell" in general, say *jag mår dåligt*; for "I'm ill", *jag är sjuk*. **moh IL-lah**.

**Trettionio och fem** — Swedish body temperature is in Celsius, and decimals are read with *och* or *komma*: *trettionio och fem* or *trettionio komma fem* (39.5 °C, about 103 °F). Normal is around 37; from 38 Swedes call it *feber*.

**Det gör ont** — "it hurts", literally "it does pain". Use it when the pain is the subject: *Det gör ont i foten*, *Gör det ont här?* (the doctor's favorite question). Swedes also say *Aj!* (Ouch!) — **ahy**.

**Halsmandlarna** — the tonsils, literally "the throat almonds". And **halsfluss** is what English calls strep throat or tonsillitis. Swedish medical words are often built from everyday parts like this, which makes them easier to guess than English Latin-based ones.

**Ett dygn** — a full twenty-four-hour period, day and night together. English has no single word for it; Swedish uses it all the time: *dygnet runt* (around the clock), *två dygn*. And **du smittar** — "you're contagious", literally "you infect". **düngn**, **SMIT-tar**.

grammars.title: Saying what's wrong
body: Swedish has a handful of fixed frames for symptoms. Learn them as wholes; the verb is not always the one English would use.

head: Frame
Example
English
rows: I have a fever / a cough / a runny nose.
I have a cold / I'm tired / dizzy.

after: Note *vara förkyld* (to have a cold) — an adjective, not a noun. *Jag **är** förkyld*, never *jag har förkyld*. The noun exists too, *en förkylning*, but the adjective is far more common.

Body parts take the definite form after *i*: *i huvud**et***, *i öra**t***, *i ben**en***. The same habit shows up elsewhere: *Han bröt arm**en*** (He broke his arm), *Tvätta händer**na**!* (Wash your hands!).

grammars.title: Modal verbs at the doctor's
body: A visit to the doctor is full of advice, permission and prohibition — perfect practice for the modals you met in Unit 11. All of them are followed by the base form, with no *att*.

head: Modal
Meaning
At the doctor
rows: Du **ska** ta en tablett på morgonen.

after: The trap from Unit 11 again: *Du måste inte komma tillbaka* would sound like a stern order to English ears but simply means "you don't have to" — and most Swedes prefer *behöver inte* for that. "You must not" is ***får inte***.

**Bör** is the present of *böra* and sounds a little more formal and objective than *borde*, which you learned in Unit 11. Doctors and official advice say *bör*; friends say *borde*: *Du borde gå till doktorn!*

blocks.text: The irregular plurals are worth learning now, because you need them all the time: *två fötter*, *båda öronen*, *ont i ögonen*, *borsta tänderna*. *Öga* and *öra* follow the same rare pattern (*-on* in the plural), as if they were a pair — which, in a way, they are.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 16
items: The doctor's instructions are full of last unit's time prepositions: *feber **i** fyra dagar* (for), *vi vet **om** tio minuter* (in, from now), *tre gånger **om** dagen*, ***i** tio dagar*.
Say three sentences about your own last cold with *i*, *på* and *för … sedan*: *Jag var förkyld för två veckor sedan. Jag hade feber i tre dagar…*

head: Where
What for
rows: Healthcare advice by phone, 24 hours a day; also the website and app where you book appointments and read your records.
Your local health center: general practitioners and nurses, for everything that isn't an emergency.
The emergency room at a hospital — only for serious cases.
The pharmacy. Prescriptions are electronic: just show your ID.

blocks.text: The Swedish way is to **call 1177 first**. A nurse asks about your symptoms and tells you whether to rest at home, book a time at the *vårdcentral* or go to *akuten*. Many people are surprised at how often the answer is "stay home, drink plenty of fluids and rest" — Swedish doctors are famously careful with antibiotics.

If you're off sick from work, you simply tell your employer (*sjukanmäla sig*). For the first seven days your word is enough; from day eight your employer needs a doctor's certificate, *ett läkarintyg*.
